publications.title: An Assistive Sensory-Based System for Integrated Fall and Obstacle Detection
publications.subtitle: IEEE
publications.description: Traditional walking canes have offered limited mobility to elderly individuals, while leaving critical safety gaps in spatial awareness and emergency response. This paper presents a novel integrated assistive system that combines obstacle detection, fall detection, biometric monitoring, and sustainable energy harvesting in a single low-cost device, helping to minimize falls in seniors without compromising comfort. The system utilizes ultrasonic sensors with haptic feedback to give the user ample time to respond to obstacles and uneven surfaces with an accuracy of 97.75% ± 1.2% (agreement with a meter-stick baseline) up to 1.5 meters and 100% detection across 27 simulated fall trials. Alongside the hardware, the companion mobile application enables real-time pulse monitoring for the user and comprehensive emergency response capabilities for caregivers. If a fall is detected by the built-in gyroscope, the location is automatically recorded in the mobile app, and an emergency call is placed to emergency services or a family member. A thermoelectric energy harvesting system converts body heat from the user’s palm into electrical energy, sustainably powering two LEDs controlled by a switch. Comprehensive testing validates the effective delivery of haptic feedback and the reliable performance of sensors with a user-adjustable detection range. Results are preliminary from bench/lab simulations; future development includes expanded user testing and baseline comparisons.

publications.title: Integrated Neuro-Symbolic Analysis Pipeline for Cerebral Aneurysm Rupture Diagnosis
publications.subtitle: Preprints
publications.description: The importance of detecting and diagnosing the imminence of aneurysm rupture before it occurs cannot be overstated. However, this process is often time-consuming and challenging, with variability in conclusions not uncommon among experts. Furthermore, current state-of-the-art models in medical image segmentation suffer from limited availability of large annotated datasets for training, exacerbated by an immense data imbalance. In most segmentation tasks, 3D segmentation is preferred due to its capacity to leverage more contextual information. However, these models require more data, which is constrained by the aforementioned issues. In the realm of current diagnosis models, those lacking geographic context are notably ineffective. To address these issues, the aim is to develop a model pipeline to accurately detect cerebral intracranial aneurysms and diagnose rupture imminence through 3D magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and tabular input, augmented with the implementation of neuro-symbolic ai. The utilization of data fusion to tackle the lack of context in tabular models is proposed, leveraging extracted geographical features from a segmentation model. To enhance segmentation results and tackle the data imbalance in aneurysm segmentation, a two-stage model pipeline that extracts contextual geographic features before aneurysm segmentation is suggested. Segmentation results are additionally improved through ensemble techniques and novel preprocessing techniques. Finally, a neuro-symbolic aspect is introduced to enhance model diagnosis, interpretability and performance. The multi-step Integrated Neuro-Symbolic Analysis Pipeline for Cerebral Aneurysm Rupture Diagnosis is introduced.

Today, we released SentinelBench, an open benchmark for agents whose main job is to wait. Most agent work assumes the agent has to keep acting to make progress. That breaks down for a big class of tasks. No amount of refreshing makes concert tickets go on sale faster. The right move is to watch, wait, and act only when the environment changes on its own. Today's agents are bad at this. They either churn on every page refresh, burning tokens and risking errors, or they give up after a few tries. SentinelBench measures exactly this. 100 tasks across 10 synthetic web apps (email, chat, a stock tracker, a music feed, and more) that evolve on their own timeline while the agent works. Some tasks are passive detection ("tell me when my post hits 100 likes"), some force the agent to keep checking, and 20 are designed to never fire, to catch agents that just declare success right before the clock runs out. How an agent waits can matter as much as which model you pick. A naive sleep-and-poll loop cost 5.1x more than a purpose-built wait_for tool at the 10-minute setting, with equal or worse accuracy. Stretch tasks to 40 minutes and the gap hits 9.7x. One sleep run cost $31 to finish a single task. As agents take on longer work, more of their time goes to waiting than acting. We think that deserves to be measured. Blog: https://lnkd.in/gjKvdTFh Code: https://lnkd.in/gR5msGCs ...more ...more

Today we're releasing SentinelBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on long-horizon monitoring tasks! Working with Microsoft AI Frontiers , we created 10 synthetic web-app environments based on familiar apps like email, social media, video and music. The goal is to test how modern LLM-based agents perform on tasks that require them to wait, monitor and act only when the right condition is met. For example, if you ask an agent to "wait until Matheus' latest LinkedIn post reaches 50 likes and notify me," it would need to first find the post, then monitor it over time, and only respond at the right moment. Testing this on real websites is hard since do not control when events happen, pages may change layout, and providers may detect and block agent traffic. SentinelBench bypasses these issues, and we're open-sourcing it so other researchers can test their own agents or adapt the environments/scenarios for their own goals. This builds on work we started last summer on agents that can wait before acting. We had an initial agent-waiting strategy but could not measure its success without a controlled benchmark. SentinelBench was built to meet that need, and we improved the strategy along the way. Huge thank you to the team: Adam Fourney , Amanda Swearngin , Hussein Mozannar , Gagan Bansal , Maya Murad , Rafah Aboul Hosn and Saleema Amershi . It has been an extremely rewarding time working with Microsoft. P.S. I'll finish my master's this fall and will be applying for PhD programs. A small CUTLASS lesson: sometimes the cleanest optimization is algebraic, not architectural. While digging deeper into FlashAttention-3 on Hopper, I came across an interesting way to think about the QKᵀ computation. The initial idea was to apply the same column permutation P to both Q and K: (QP)(KP)ᵀ = QPPᵀKᵀ = QKᵀ Because P is orthogonal, the permutation cancels exactly. No approximation, no change to the mathematical result. The motivation was purely from the memory side. On Hopper, I was thinking about whether a shared permutation could make Q and K tiles easier to place in a compatible TMA swizzle layout, potentially simplifying parts of the producer pipeline and reducing layout management. But there is a much cleaner way to look at the same problem. In inference kernels, this is often handled through swap AB. Instead of physically transforming the data, you can change how the GEMM operands are interpreted. The transpose is handled algebraically rather than by moving or permuting memory. Working more seriously with CUTLASS, this became much more concrete. A matrix stored in row-major layout can represent the same physical data as its transpose in column-major layout. Nothing needs to be moved. You can effectively change the interpretation through the layout or stride descriptor. CUTLASS makes this visible through LayoutA and LayoutB, while CuTe takes the idea even further by treating layouts as first-class objects. So what initially looked like a complicated memory-layout optimization can often be reframed as a descriptor-level transformation. That distinction is important when writing high-performance GPU kernels: Don't move data if you can change the way the computation interprets it. There is still an interesting Hopper-specific question here. WGMMA imposes fairly strict requirements on the physical layout of its A and B operands. So while the algebraic swap itself is free, the resulting shared-memory layout, swizzling, and operand arrangement may not always be free. That makes the boundary between: algebraic transformation → layout transformation → physical data movement a particularly interesting place to reason about when optimizing Hopper kernels. The more I work with CUTLASS and CuTe, the more I appreciate that high-performance GPU programming is often less about inventing new mathematics and more about finding the representation where the existing mathematics maps cleanly onto the hardware. #CUDA #CUTLASS #CuTe #GPUProgramming #FlashAttention #FlashAttention3 #HopperGPU #WGMMA #TMA #LLMInference #InferenceOptimization #DeepLearning #PerformanceEngineering

Our compiler is finding insanely fast megakernels. Luminal searches through a massive space of possible megakernels and finds ones that push overlapping and bandwidth / flop utilization as far as possible. These results are without extra quantization or speculative decoding. Megakernels overcome some big limitations with traditional kernel graphs by giving us much more flexible schedules not bound by a normal kernel grid. We can immediately kick off work the moment it's inputs are ready, or even partially load inputs before other inputs are ready. This flexibility demands very large-scale search to max out the GPU resources. Luminal is a search-based compiler. That means we build a search space, and iterate through tons of generated implementations to find the fastest ones. Every scheduling decision, instruction, main loop, all get searched and chosen amongst millions of possibilities. We wanted to see if we could add megakernels to the search space. Luminal was designed from the start to use extremely flexible representations to target heterogeneous hardware, so we've been able to add megakernel generation alongside traditional kernel generation, in the same search space. This overcomes one of the key traditional limitations with megakernels: they can't re-use the ecosystem of high-performance kernels already written. By constructing a unified search space, we're able to search across both traditional kernels and megakernel ops to discover the optimal mixes. There's a ton of stuff we had to invent to bring megakernels from the lab to production, so I'm giving a talk with GPU MODE in a few weeks!

in honor of the Rubin spec sheet coming out, i'll be doing a series on Rubin's low level software. starting with a GUIDE on HOW TO ACTUALLY READ AN NVIDIA SPEC SHEET: nvidia's headline for rubin is 50 petaflops of nvfp4, 5x blackwell. the dense number is 35. the word "sparse" appears nowhere on the spec page. you have to open the pdf datasheet, where footnote 1 ends with five words: "NVFP4 Inference specification is sparse." FIVE CORE RULES to decode any nvidia spec sheet. rule 1: find the density basis. every headline AI number since a100 assumes 2:4 structured sparsity. in 2020 the dense number came first: "156 TF | 312 TF*". h100 flipped the order in 2022, then quietly deleted the dense column: "Shown with sparsity. Specifications are one-half lower without sparsity." blackwell launched at 20 petaflops of fp4 with no dense number on the page, just a two word footnote: "With sparsity." and the sparse premium isn't 2x anymore. gb300 is 20 sparse vs 15 dense. rubin is 50 vs 35, and the 35 is labeled "training". a dense inference number for rubin does not exist anywhere. rule 2: match the precision on both sides of any Nx. a100's "20x volta" was sparse tf32 tensor ops against v100's fp32 cuda cores. same unit and same precision, the gain was 2.5x. h100's "30x" ran fp8 against fp16, on 32 a100s vs 16 h100s, at batch 4 vs 60. blackwell's "30x h100" was fp4 vs fp8. rubin's "5x blackwell" compares compressed 50 against dense 10. dense to dense it's 3.5x, the biggest like-for-like gain in years. but it's 3.5, not 5. rule 3: ask what "one GPU" means. blackwell is two dies sold as one gpu. at gtc 2025 jensen said that naming "was wrong" and the rubin rack debuted as NVL144, counting dies. at ces 2026 it became NVL72 again, counting packages. same rack, same silicon, both names. the only acknowledgment is an editor's note retrofitted onto an old blog post. even one b200 has three official fp4 ratings: 20 petaflops grace-paired, 18 on hgx boards, 14 in b100. all sparse, obviously. rule 4: "up to" means one point on a curve. rubin's "10x tokens per megawatt" chart is real. the 10x arrow is drawn above 200 tokens/sec/user, exactly where blackwell's curve collapses. the left edge of the same chart reads 1.7x. every generation runs this play: gb300's "50x vs hopper" is 10x responsiveness times 5x throughput, multiplied together right on the product page. rule 5: the footnotes never lie. rubin's 200 teraflops of fp64? footnote 3: "Peak performance using Tensor Core-based emulation algorithms." native fp64 is 33 teraflops, down from blackwell's 40. and the spec sheet has no power row at all, not for the gpu, not for the rack, so every tokens-per-megawatt denominator is unauditable. none of this is hidden btw! the real numbers are all there, in the fine print. nvidia is rigorous about footnotes precisely because the headlines are doing so much work.

There are 3 basic levels of computer code in the NVIDIA software stack CUDA C++, PTX, and SASS Understanding all 3 helps you know why CUDA is so useful CUDA C++ - It gives you NVIDIA’s programming model (threads, blocks, shared memory, synchronization) without requiring you to write instructions for just an exact GPU architecture. In fact, a good CUDA kernel is often used across multiple generations of NVIDIA hardware. You just get less of the cutting edge performance out of the newer hardware when you reuse kernels CUDA C++ is lowered into PTX PTX (Parallel Thread Execution) - This is a virtual instruction set. Because they are virtual machine instructions, they allow one CUDA kernel to run across different NVIDIA devices without needing to be rewritten. That being said when we want to use a specific command on a specific part of a chip (like a WGMMA), we will specify it in PTX so that there is no confusion during compilation about what we want to use. Naturally, this choice comes with the trade-off of portability. Once we specify exactly what hardware component we want, we cannot port that kernel to an NVIDIA device that doesn't have that component PTX is lowered to SASS SASS - NVIDIA's native machine code. This is the end of the road. We take our virtual instruction set and bring it down into the exact executable code that will run on our specific machine. This is the least portable version of the code, but of course the most complete CUDA's great advantage is that you can take a kernel written for Ampere and move it to Hopper on launch day. This lets NVIDIA's software stack compound The challenge is the abstraction. By giving this distance, you rely heavily on your NVIDIA compilers to find fast ways to run your code on different hardware In practice, a developer will try many different strategies to find the fastest way to run their kernel In other words, you have to do a manual search At Luminal, we're creating a compiler that will handle this search entirely automatically and deterministically

Hi everyone :) I don't normally post on LinkedIn, but I wanted to share an experience I had recently with a company I interviewed with through WaterlooWorks. In keeping this as factual as possible, I applied to a Cerebras co-op role that was advertised as having one open position. After my interview I received an informal offer, proceeded to decline another interview offer along with another external offer from another company, then later learned the one spot on WaterlooWorks went to someone else. That sequence caused a lot of wasted effort and stress. After having a conversation with the recruiter, I learned that the reason I did not ultimately receive the offer was because I did not commit fully to them upon receiving my informal offer. However, I had no idea the offer was conditional upon this, as this fact was not shared with me. In fact, it has repeatedly been encouraged by CECA, the co-op program itself, for students to weigh their options carefully before deciding on rankings. As a result, I was unable to receive a match through WaterlooWorks this cycle. I do feel upset, but ultimately, I’m sharing this so other students (especially those in Waterloo’s co-op program) know how critical it is to not assume that an informal offer is final. This experience highlighted for me how damaging miscommunication can be in co-op recruiting. I’m still seeking a Fall 2025 placement. If anyone knows of openings for a 3A Computer Science student skilled in the fields of linear algebra/robotics/computer vision/performance computing, I’d be grateful for any referrals. Apple's Q.ai acquisition signals a shift in human-device interaction Too often I hear that Apple lost the AI race. I wouldn't bet on that. Apple was always great at watching what happens and then making the right decisions. Not by being the first or the fastest. The acquisition of Q.ai could hint at an interesting perspective on how we might interact with devices one day. Apple has acquired Israeli AI startup Q.ai for nearly $2 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company's history (after Beats at $3 billion). What makes this different isn't just the price tag. It's the technology and intent behind it. Q.ai specializes in "silent speech" systems that interpret facial micro-movements and non-spoken interaction cues. That's a fundamental shift in how we might communicate with devices, moving beyond touch and voice to something far more intuitive. From a strategic lens, this matters because: AI becomes a hardware differentiator. Not just software or cloud services. This technology is built for AirPods, Vision Pro, and future wearables. Human-centric design meets AI interpretation. A new frontier in UX. Think: conversing with Siri in a crowded room without speaking, or accessibility breakthroughs for people with speech impairments. Strategic acquisition over build. Apple builds internally when it makes sense, but buys when they see technology that fits their long-term vision and proven teams they can integrate. Proven leadership matters. Q.ai CEO Aviad Maizels previously sold PrimeSense to Apple in 2013, which became the foundation for Face ID. Apple knows what they're getting. Where this could go: AirPods that understand whispered commands or mouthed words. Vision Pro that responds to facial expressions without hand gestures. Accessibility features for people who can't speak. And yes, potentially a Siri that finally understands context without requiring "Hey Siri" every time. In a world where engagement and attention are currency, the ability to decode subtle intent could become a powerful interface. Can't wait to experience this tech in one of my future Apple devices!

This summer, one of my goals was to become more industry-ready by building skills beyond the classroom and developing a deeper understanding of modern AI frameworks and their real-world possibilities. As part of that journey, I built ContextCue - an agentic AI system that transforms recorded meetings into searchable, persistent, and actionable organizational memory. Your team’s memory, on cue. Most meeting tools treat each meeting as an isolated transcript or summary. I wanted to explore a broader idea: meetings should contribute to a continuously accessible layer of organizational knowledge. Important decisions often become separated from the reasoning behind them. Action items lose context, unresolved questions are forgotten, and teams struggle to reconstruct why a direction was chosen weeks or months later. Consider a business executive preparing for a client follow-up. They may remember that a pricing proposal was rejected, but not the client’s exact concern, the alternatives discussed, or who agreed to revise it. Instead of searching through recordings, notes, emails, and chats, they could ask: “Why was the original pricing proposal rejected, what alternative was discussed, and what did we agree to do next?” ContextCue retrieves relevant information across meetings, generates a grounded response with timestamp citations, identifies related action items and open questions, and can prepare a contextual follow-up. The same idea could help engineering teams track technical decisions, consulting and sales teams retain client context, research groups follow evolving findings, and project handoffs preserve reasoning that might otherwise be lost. The system can: • Search semantically across meetings • Retrieve decisions and supporting discussions • Generate grounded answers with timestamp citations • Identify action items, owners, and open questions • Prepare follow-ups using previous context • Preserve continuity across recurring conversations What interested me most was not simply building another transcription or meeting-summary tool, but exploring how AI could preserve the reasoning, commitments, and context behind organizational decisions. The system uses an agent layer with intent routing and tool-based retrieval. I also built an evaluation workflow to verify that relevant context is retrieved before generating a response, since reliable retrieval is essential for trustworthy AI. Built with Python, FastAPI, Faster-Whisper, Qdrant, Ollama, Streamlit, FFmpeg, RAG, SQLite, MCP, and vector search. There is still so much more I want to build, improve, and learn through this project. I’m excited to keep experimenting and expanding ContextCue. A special thank you to my mentor, Rajeshwari Ganesan , for her guidance, feedback, and support. Excited to share that our paper, "Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning," has been accepted to the ICLR (International Conference on Learning Representations) 2026 LIT Workshop! 🎉 As AI systems are deployed in high-stakes settings such as medicine, law, finance, we rely on their explanations to catch errors and verify decisions. But if a model can reach the right answer while ignoring its own stated reasoning, those explanations can't be trusted as a window into its behavior. Transparency tools built on top of flawed reasoning chains may give false confidence to the people relying on them. The core finding: high accuracy doesn't mean a model actually uses its reasoning chain. We introduce NLDD, a metric that measures whether corrupting individual CoT steps changes model confidence, and discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens contribute nothing (or actively hurt). Gemma hit 99% accuracy on logical inference while exhibiting negative NLDD. It was getting the right answer despite its own reasoning, not because of it. Huge thanks to my incredible co-authors Max Loffgren , Om Kotadia , Linus Wong , and mentor Jonas Rohweder — and to Kevin Zhu and the entire Algoverse AI Research team . publications.title: Co-author
publications.description: Training computer use agents requires full-featured OS sandboxes with GUI environments, which consume substantial hardware resources as the number of sandboxes scales. Stochastic errors arising from diverse software execution within these sandboxes further demand robust infrastructure design and reliable error recovery. We present OSGym, a scalable OS environment infrastructure for computer use agents, built around these key optimization strategies: (1) Decentralized OS state management, which isolates failures to individual replicas and significantly enhances overall system reliability; (2) Hardware-aware OS replica orchestration, which addresses CPU-bounded scaling bottlenecks and substantially reduces compute overhead; (3) KVM virtualization with copy-on-write disk management, which shares a common bootable disk across VM instances and provisions only instance-specific modifications, reducing physical disk consumption by 88% and increasing disk provisioning speed by 37 times; and (4) Robust container pool with multi-layer fault recovery. Together, these optimizations yield strong scalability and resource efficiency: OSGym manages over a thousand OS replicas under constrained resources, supports parallel trajectory generation at 1420 multi-turn trajectories per minute, and reduces per-replica cost to 0.2-0.3 USD per day, a 90% reduction over standard deployment. Our experiments validate OSGym across end-to-end pipelines for data collection and training for computer use agents. We believe OSGym establishes a new foundation for scalable, general-purpose computer use agent research.

publications.description: This paper proposes using the YOLO object detection algorithm to accurately and efficiently detect nuts and screws using a custom-built 6-DOF robotic arm equipped with a gripper and a depth camera running the YOLO v10 object detection model in real-time, addressing the challenges of traditional detection methods in fast-paced production environments. This capability enables subsequent robot control to dynamically adjust actions based on precise component localization. Dynamic control in robotic automation has traditionally depended on model-based approaches, where performance depends on accurate system modeling. However, as systems grow more complex, precise modeling becomes increasingly challenging, often leading to suboptimal control. To address these limitations, we propose an Adaptive Robust Learning (ARL) Control algorithm. By integrating a Disturbance Observer (DOB) within the ILC framework, the ARL Control algorithm enhances adaptability and robustness, compensating for real-time disturbances. This work highlights the potential of combining advanced control algorithms with state-of-the-art visual recognition in robotics, paving the way for robust learning solutions in dynamic environments.

projects.title: Geometry-Aware Positional Embeddings for 3D Object Reconstruction
projects.description: We developed a geometry-aware Transformer pipeline for reconstructing 3D objects from sparse 2D views.Most 2D-to-3D reconstruction systems treat image patches mainly as visual tokens with 2D positional information. Our project studied whether adding explicit camera geometry helps a Transformer reason about how those patches correspond to 3D space. We compared standard 2D positional embeddings, learned View-ID embeddings, camera-pose embeddings, and ray-aware embeddings while keeping the encoder, fusion module, decoder, dataset, and evaluation protocol fixed.Our strongest model augmented each ViT patch token with the camera origin and per-patch viewing ray before multi-view Transformer fusion. This let the model treat each patch as a camera-grounded 3D observation rather than just a location in an image grid.We evaluated on a controlled ShapeNetCore subset of approximately 2,000 objects across K={1,2,4,8,16} input views, predicting 2,048-point surface point clouds and measuring Chamfer Distance and F-score. Geometry-aware embeddings achieved the best performance across all view counts, with the largest gains in sparse-view settings: 17% lower Chamfer error at K=1 and 22% lower Chamfer error at K=2 compared to the 2D positional baseline.

projects.title: From Text to Torque: Improving RL Tracking of Text-Generated Humanoid Motions
projects.description: Text-conditioned motion generators can synthesize plausible humanoid trajectories, but these kinematic references may not be dynamically feasible for torque-controlled robots. We study this gap using KimoLab, which connects Kimodo text-generated Unitree G1 motions to MuJoCo Warp PPO tracking.Across walking, waving, tapping the head, squatting, and harder generated prompts, we find that termination design strongly affects whether PPO observes enough of the reference to learn stable tracking. Gesture-like motions and walking remain learnable under strict termination, but one squat reference seed collapses to short episodes under default strict thresholds.A gradual termination curriculum localizes the failure boundary, and direct calibrated-threshold training recovers full-horizon squat tracking from scratch. Adaptive threshold calibration selects the successful threshold automatically, while simple reference smoothing and initial-pose holds do not rescue strict training.

projects.title: Language Learning as a Sequential Decision-Making Problem
projects.description: Built an adaptive language tutoring system that frames exercise selection as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). Using the Duolingo SLAM dataset with ~4.8M token-level interactions, we calibrated a simulated learner through maximum likelihood estimation of an item response theory model, then trained and compared six tutoring policies: PPO, DQN, MPC, LinUCB, curriculum-based sequencing, and random baselines.Our best model using PPO achieved the strongest cost-adjusted reward by dynamically balancing cheap practice modules with more expensive, higher-effectiveness exercises. Model predictive control matched PPO’s final proficiency but required higher cost, showing that long-horizon planning improves adaptive tutoring decisions over myopic or hand-designed curricula.

projects.title: Pi Invaders
projects.description: A ground‑up re‑creation of Space Invaders that runs on a 1 GHz RISC‑V Mango Pi without an OS.Derek, Zach and I integrate low-level libraries relating to GPIO, UART, I²C, PCM, DMA, I²S, SPI and more to enable users to shoot using microphone input, move the spaceship in real time through an accelerometer and hear audio play as aliens get destroyed. The game loop is kept responsive in real-time through interrupt‑driven, lock‑free queues. The result is an arcade‑style game with multimodal inputs driven entirely by low‑level C and direct register pokes.

Inspired by the philosophy of ichi-go ichi-e (one time, one meeting), we focused on making remote conversations more meaningful and immersive. We integrated Zoom’s API with multimodal AI models Groq, OpenAI, Gemini, and ElevenLabs to analyze live speech, gestures, and sentiment. The system responds with a personalized AI avatar and dynamic meeting environments powered by Luma AI. Our backend tracked user attention, mood, and behavior to adapt the tone and atmosphere of the meeting in real time.

projects.title: Trumpet Controlled Nerf Turret
projects.description: Chisa and I built a real-time, audio-responsive turret system that rotates and fires a Nerf gun based on trumpet notes. We integrated a Raspberry Pi 5 with a stepper motor and solenoid actuator, processing microphone input using FFT to detect specific frequencies. Each note triggered a unique hardware action, rotating the turret clockwise, counterclockwise, or firing. The project involved low-level GPIO programming with lgpio, mechanical integration using 3D-printed parts, and real-time audio signal processing in Python.

Before I could even understand what developmental disabilities were, Sitara (Akka) has been just like any other older sister. In my earliest memories, she kept me safe when I was afraid of the dark, offered me company as I would practice music, and scolded me if I didn't brush my teeth in the morning. Akka's personality is one-of-a-kind, full of sarcastic humor and clever comebacks that stay in our minds even decades later. Her routines have become our family's routines, whether it was Jeopardy every day at 7 PM, water at 10:30, 2:30, and 5:30, or her post-lunch walk which she would do daily, without fail. Akka taught me so much: compassion, discipline, and above all, resilience, how someone could overcome so many medical challenges with the utmost patience and calm, and bounce back each time with renewed vigor and energy. She has seen me grow throughout all stages of my life -- when I was born, when I graduated high school, and now when I graduated college, and she will continue to watch over our family for our lives to come. Akka's presence has touched our family and so many others throughout her 38 beautiful years, and through her strength she has inspired us consistently to become the best version of ourselves. I can't imagine what it will be like to go on without you, Akka, but wherever you are, I hope you have all your favorite snacks, foods, and books beside you, and may you find liberation in the Lotus Feet of the Lord.

AI is being used wrong in audit. The new tools make audit faster. Faster testing. Faster review. Faster workpapers. But the problem is deeper than speed. Audit still operates the old way, where auditors wait for the quarter to end, then go look at what already happened. That approach was built around a constraint that no longer holds: human teams couldn’t keep up with everything happening inside a company. That’s not true anymore. All other functions in a company have modernized, but audit still runs on the old model. And the cost of that is bigger than people realize. CPAs are aging out, fewer students are entering the field, and the work that’s left is the grunt work that drove people away in the first place. Making that work faster doesn’t fix it. At Arden (YC P26) , we believe audit should run continuously, where the AI surfaces issues as they happen, and the auditors bring judgment. That’s what auditors actually signed up to do.

Some Thursdays you just bike downtown, leading a group of friends with Audrey Pozen , to see an exhibit you helped curate finally open to the public. Today was one of those days! "Freedom to Thrive: The American Experiment in Colorado Springs" just opened at the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum , and getting to contribute to it through my Community Based Research course in the Sociology Department at Colorado College was one of my favorite parts of this past school year. activity.title: Open weight models are supposed to close the gap with the frontier labs. And the weights really are open. The alignment is not. Nobody ships a list of what a model was post-trained to refuse. So you find it the way I did. I built a bot that writes my morning news brief. 130 headlines in, a 60,000 character PDF out. Last week it delivered one empty page. I assumed auth, because it had been auth before. It wasn't. HTTP 200, valid response, 13 characters of Chinese saying it could not provide the content. finish_reason=content_filter. DeepSeek had not failed. It had declined. So I tested it: take a bundle it writes happily, inject one suspect headline, repeat. "India Names 27 Places in Arunachal Pradesh | Counters China's Renaming Claims" With that headline, 8 of 12 calls refused. Without it, 0 of 12. Then I went looking for the boundary and could not find it. A Taiwan tensions headline from the same feed: 0 of 8. A written-to-order headline of Taiwan's president declaring the island sovereign and rejecting Beijing's claim: 0 of 3. The same Arunachal sentence with China swapped for Britain and the Falklands: 0 of 3. Not the topic. Not the region. Not the framing. That one story. Open weight feels like control. Download it, self host it, switch providers, no vendor policy layer in the way. All true of the infrastructure. None of it true of the model. No setting, no policy page, no support ticket, and switching providers changes nothing, because it was never the provider's rule. You are not just picking a model. You are picking whose regulatory environment decided what it will write about. In a chat window you would never notice. In an automated pipeline it is an empty page at 8am. Two thirds of the time, for one headline out of 130. ...more

The SF hackathon run is off to a good start. We took 1st place at the Loop Engineering Hackathon hosted by tokens& at the AWS Builder Loft (best hackathon venue i've been to yet). 250 people, 100 projects, one afternoon to build something worth winning. The idea started simple but got sharper as we went. We built Vigil: an AI on-call engineer that detects, diagnoses, and rolls back production incidents while holding zero standing credentials. Every other agent demo right now is a race to hand the model everything, more keys, more access, more scope, so we inverted that. Vigil holds nothing at rest. Every destructive action gets a single-use credential scoped to one service, expiring in literally 60 seconds. Zero sells it a log parser per call, Overclock Labs, creators of Akash Network runs a disposable sandbox that reproduces the failure before anything touches production (which won us best use), Pomerium gates every rollback against policy, and OpenAI adds a root-cause hypothesis on top. When Vigil later tried a mass-restart across 12 services, the gate denied it. That denial is the whole thesis. The model never gets trusted, it gets contained. That's least-privilege for autonomous agents, shown end to end. Shoutout to Dat and Pranav and their Claude max subscriptions. feat. drippiest duck in sf ...more

GMI posted something this week that stuck with me: instead of relying on one frontier model, you run Opus 4.8 first and let GLM 5.2 clean up what it misses. 94/100 pass rate, 47% cheaper than Fable 5. The hack reported by OpenAI and Hugging Face is a direct result of the lack of data quality practices coming from RL environments. RLVR is an extremely powerful tool that has brought us into superhuman coding agents and more. But that’s the problem: They are extremely powerful optimizers, and will do anything to receive a reward. Every benchmark, every RL environment, and every verifier is a potential attack surface. Even SWE-bench Verified had a bug in it for over one and a half years where part of the GitHub history was leaking. What have we done about this? 1. We published a paper back in April about verifying the verifiers. We were the first to do so. 2. We released SWE-Marathon, which is focusing on reward hacking in the ultra-long horizon setting. 3. We published blog posts about reward hacking and are working with numerous partners to increase visibility of this issue. There’s a lot more work to be done here. Excited to share that our paper “Programmable Quantum Matter: Heralding Large Cluster States in Driven Inhomogeneous Spin Ensembles” is now on arXiv: https://lnkd.in/e9R2uHqx One of the biggest challenges in scaling quantum systems at low temperatures (10 mK–1 K) is heat-induced decoherence. When control pulses arrive faster than the thermalization timescale of qubit’s local environment, local temperature rises and coherence is lost — directly limiting how many qubits can be operated simultaneously. In this work, we introduce a framework that turns a supposed weakness — inhomogeneities in spin ensembles (SiV color centers) — into a resource. Using global control, phase denoising, thermal modeling, and a modified single-photon entanglement protocol, we show how large entangled cluster states can be generated efficiently. An interesting coincidence is that, this project began 1.5 years ago, inspired by Dirk’s cantilever-based idea posted below, and only few months back did we discover that the term “Programmable Matter” was first introduced here at MIT 35 years ago by Prof. Tommaso Toffoli and Prof. Norman Margolus — in the context of cellular automata based multiprocessors. There’s a deep connection between cellular automata and entangled cluster states too… but that’s for the next time. Grateful to Prof. Dirk Englund for this opportunity and to my amazing colleagues Louis Follet and Odiel Hooybergs . This is joint work with Ángel David Reyero Lobo , Denis A. Engemann , and Bertrand Thirion . 🎯 Explainable AI promises to reveal what complex models, often considered black boxes, learn during training, thereby increasing trust in their predictions. For instance, explaining a model trained to predict disease risk from large clinical cohorts can help identify new risk factors and ways to prevent disease. ⚠️ However, complex AI models are prone to instability, making them hard to interpret; small perturbations in training can change the inner workings of these models. This phenomenon is known as the Rashomon effect. It was named after a movie depicting conflicting witness accounts of the same incident during a trial. 💡 We study how best to mitigate this effect. Should we aggregate the explanations of multiple models, or explain a single larger model that itself aggregates predictions? Our analysis reveals that the second approach is more effective, providing practitioners with a simple guideline for obtaining more reliable explanations from complex models. 🎬 To pursue the analogy: should multiple juries each hear one witness and then aggregate their verdicts, or should a single jury hear all witnesses and deliver one verdict? link: https://lnkd.in/ePJBH3sy pdf: https://lnkd.in/eP9a4YPh

activity.title: Last week, I led a UX Workshop at work ( Google !) on how to ship your side projects as a designer, with 400+ viewers — with how fast AI is evolving, it's now easier than ever to build and create. But many designers are still super intimidated by the technical side of things or don't know how to get started. I've shipped several consumer side projects to 13k+ users, and have learned a lot along the way — so here's a practical step-by-step guide on how to ship 0-1, modified from my workshop slides! 💡1: Ideation Brainstorming with AI can be pretty awesome. I'm NOT saying to let AI take over your idea; you should definitely use your own creativity. But it can be a fantastic resource for expanding on your thoughts! 🎨 2: Designing I always design first in Figma — but in my opinion, the no. 1 mistake is letting yourself get stuck in the weeds and endlessly iterating because you want your designs to be perfect. Figure out if your goal is shipping or creating a "perfect" product. 🤖 3: Where to build? Vibe coding platforms (Lovable, Replit) are visual first and auto-configure your infrastructure for you, but are not great for complexity. I strongly prefer coding agents (Claude, Codex) for full flexibility and because MCPs instantly solve the problem of configuring/setting up infrastructure etc. 🧑‍💻 4: Setting up You can send a prompt like: "I'm not very technical but I want to build ABC. Help me figure out my tech stack, feasibility of each feature, and how to set up the necessary infrastructure." Ask your agent to connect MCPs to automate the setup! Remember, you can ask for step-by-step instructions for literally anything at any point in time. 🔨 5: Building! Ask your agent to create a plan with multiple stages of development (e.g. MVP features, then auth, then nice-to-have features). For each stage, have a self-contained prompt that can be pasted into a new session to kick off development. Makes this super easy! 🪲 6: Testing & bug-bashing 1. "Spin up multiple subagents to do a comprehensive audit of each part of the codebase." 2. "Use Playwright to walk through my user flows and ensure the flows operate as intended." 3. "Imagine you're XYZ. Simulate using the app and give me a report." 🚀 7: Time to deploy Again, you can just ask your agent for step-by-step instructions. Popular options are Vercel and Cloudflare. With MCPs, you can get your project off localhost in 1 minute — you will need to do this to share your projects with other people. 🦔 8: Adding analytics! I think analytics are so helpful and teach you so much about how to optimize and improve. I absolutely love PostHog — you can watch session replays of users interacting with your UI, create custom insights (not just vanity metrics like MAU), etc. 🌐 9: GTM Figure out where your target users are. This summer, I had the opportunity to attend the XX International Summer Space School in Samara, Russia! Here at Samara State Aerospace University , I led an international, cross-disciplinary team of students, researchers, and PhD-level scientists in designing a SamSat-LED 3U CubeSat mission. Our team focused on designing an LED-based optical backup communication payload using Manchester encoding. I worked through the full engineering pipeline, supervising and contributing to the link budget analysis, power budgeting, solar panel sizing, and apparent magnitude calculations to assess optical downlink feasibility. Furthermore, we built an FSM-based health monitoring architecture integrating battery, temperature, and solar subsystems.
